familyProfiles/anglican/tagline: Catholic and Reformed, held together by common prayer and bishops.
familyProfiles/anglican/summary: The churches descended from the Church of England, most of them members of the Anglican Communion. They keep bishops in historic succession and the creeds, worship from the Book of Common Prayer tradition, and combine Catholic, Reformed and evangelical strands.
familyProfiles/anglican/story:
The Church of England separated from Rome when Henry VIII, refused an annulment of his marriage, had Parliament declare him Supreme Head of the Church (Act of Supremacy, 1534). Under Edward VI, Archbishop Thomas Cranmer gave it Protestant doctrine and the Book of Common Prayer (1549, 1552); after Mary I's Catholic restoration, the Elizabethan Settlement (1559) and the Thirty-Nine Articles (1571) set a Reformed but episcopal church, defended by Richard Hooker.

The tradition spread with English colonisation and emigration, and then through missionary societies such as the SPG (1701) and the Church Missionary Society (1799). After American independence the Episcopal Church (1789) became the first Anglican church outside the British Isles; colonial churches later became self-governing provinces. The first Lambeth Conference of bishops met in 1867.

Internal tensions have been constant. Puritans wanted further reform; the Nonjurors refused to swear allegiance to William III (1689); Methodism grew within and then outside the church; the Oxford Movement (1833) revived Catholic teaching and ritual, provoking evangelical opposition. Since the 1970s the ordination of women and disagreements over sexuality have strained the Communion, leading to the Global Anglican Future Conference (GAFCON, 2008), the Anglican Church in North America (2009), and in 2025 GAFCON's declaration that it would no longer recognise the Archbishop of Canterbury as the Communion's focus of unity.

The Anglican Communion is commonly described as having some 85 million members in 42 provinces, a figure based largely on baptismal rolls; regular worshippers are far fewer in England. The largest and fastest-growing provinces are in Africa, especially Nigeria, Uganda and Kenya, while the churches in Britain, North America and Australia are shrinking.

Anglicanism's influence comes above all from the Book of Common Prayer and the King James Bible (1611), which shaped the English language, from its choral and hymn traditions, and from its model of a 'via media'. Methodism and much of the Episcopal-style church order of the Global South grew from it, and the Church of South India (1947) was the first union of episcopal and non-episcopal churches.

familyProfiles/anabaptist/tagline: Believers' baptism, discipleship and the way of peace.
familyProfiles/anabaptist/summary: The 'radical Reformation' churches—Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites, Brethren and others—that baptise only confessing believers, follow the Sermon on the Mount, reject violence and stress a church separate from the state.
familyProfiles/anabaptist/story:
Anabaptism began in Zurich on 21 January 1525, when Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz and George Blaurock, disappointed that Zwingli would not abolish infant baptism, baptised one another as adults. Their opponents called them 'Anabaptists' (re-baptisers). The Schleitheim Confession (1527) set out their convictions: believers' baptism, church discipline, separation from the world, refusal of the sword and of oaths.

Persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike, thousands were executed, Manz being drowned in the Limmat in 1527. The movement spread through Switzerland, South Germany, Austria, Moravia and the Netherlands. The violent episode of the Anabaptist kingdom at Münster (1534–35) discredited the name, and the former priest Menno Simons gathered the scattered peaceful Anabaptists of the Low Countries from 1536, giving the Mennonites their name.

The tradition divided over discipline and separation. Hutterites (from 1528) practised community of goods; the Amish followed Jakob Ammann in 1693 in insisting on strict 'shunning'; the Brethren of Schwarzenau (1708) combined Anabaptism with Pietism. Seeking religious freedom, groups migrated to Pennsylvania, Russia, Canada, Mexico, Paraguay and Bolivia, many retaining German dialects.

The Mennonite World Conference's 2018 census counted about 2.13 million baptised Anabaptist members in 86 countries; Africa (notably the DR Congo, Ethiopia's Meserete Kristos Church, Tanzania and Kenya) now has more members than North America. The Amish and Old Order groups in the United States are growing fast through large families. India has Mennonite and Brethren in Christ churches, mostly in Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Bihar.

Anabaptists pioneered the idea of a voluntary church free from state control and of religious liberty, and their peace witness inspired conscientious objection and relief work (Mennonite Central Committee, 1920). The twentieth-century 'Anabaptist vision' of Harold Bender and John Howard Yoder's The Politics of Jesus (1972) influenced many evangelicals and other Christians.
familyProfiles/anabaptist/origin/event: Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz and George Blaurock perform the first adult baptisms of the Swiss Brethren.

familyProfiles/baptist/tagline: Believers' baptism, congregational freedom and religious liberty.
familyProfiles/baptist/summary: Congregational Protestant churches that baptise believers by immersion, hold Scripture as the final authority and defend the autonomy of the local church and freedom of conscience. They range from Calvinist to Arminian and from very conservative to liberal.
familyProfiles/baptist/story:
Baptists emerged among English Separatists in exile. In Amsterdam in 1609 John Smyth baptised himself and his congregation as believers; his colleague Thomas Helwys returned to found the first Baptist church in England at Spitalfields (1612) and wrote a famous plea for religious liberty. These 'General' Baptists were Arminian; 'Particular' Baptists, Calvinist, appeared in London in the 1630s, and their London Confession (1644) adopted immersion.

In America Roger Williams founded a Baptist church at Providence (1638/9), and the Great Awakening produced the Separate Baptists, who spread rapidly across the South and among enslaved Africans, who formed their own churches. William Carey's Baptist Missionary Society (1792) and his work at Serampore launched the modern missionary movement; Adoniram Judson took the faith to Burma, and Baptists later became the largest church in Nagaland and much of north-east India.

Congregational independence made division easy. Baptists split over slavery when the Southern Baptist Convention formed in 1845; Black Baptists organised the National Baptist Convention (1895). There were divisions over missions (Primitive Baptists), the Sabbath (Seventh Day Baptists), Landmarkism, the authority of Scripture (Spurgeon's Downgrade controversy, 1887) and, in the Southern Baptist Convention after 1979, a 'conservative resurgence' that led moderates to form the Cooperative Baptist Fellowship (1991).

The Baptist World Alliance reported about 47 million baptised members in 241 member bodies in 2021; because Baptists count only baptised believers, the wider community is larger. The largest concentrations are in the United States, Nigeria, Brazil, the DR Congo, India's north-east, Myanmar and South Korea.

Baptists have been leading advocates of religious liberty and church–state separation, from Helwys to the First Amendment's supporters, and produced figures such as Spurgeon, Billy Graham and Martin Luther King Jr. Their congregational model shaped much of modern evangelical and independent Christianity.
